 1                                     I.       INTRODUCTION

 2     Q.   PLEASE IDENTIFY YOURSELF AND THE PURPOSE OF THIS CROSS-

 3          REBUTTAL TESTIMONY.

 4     A.   My name is Aaron Brewer. I provided direct testimony on behalf of Save the Lampasas,

 5          Carpenter Land and Cattle Co, Martin, and the N3 Opposition Landowner Group,

 6          collectively referred to as Landowner Group. Upon review of the direct testimony

 7          provided by others, new information and arguments were identified that prompted this

 8          cross-rebuttal, provided on behalf of the Landowner Group.


 9     Q.   WHAT TOPICS WILL YOU ADDRESS IN THIS CROSS-REBUTTAL?

10     A.   Direct testimony provided by others brought up several topics worth evaluation. In this cross-

11          rebuttal testimony I address arguments regarding the Colorado River crossings, impacts

12          to Texas Parks & Wildlife parks, a proposed modification to Link J24, concerns for

13          links and routes that impact golden-cheeked warbler, archeological concerns for Link


       CROSS-REBUTTAL TESTIMONY                                                      AARON BREWER
                                                                                               Page 4 of 14



 1             K41 and G51, and concerns regarding potential impacts to wildlife and habitat. In

 2             addressing these concerns, I note deficiencies with the "best meets" route put forward

 3             by some expert witnesses and provide additional support to rebut assertions that Route

 4             894, or other routes using Link U3 are supeiior to Route 572.

 5        IL        CROSS-REBUTTAL OF TESTIMONY REGARDING OPTIONS FOR
 6                          CROSSING THE COLORADO RIVER

 7   Q.        PLEASE       DESCRIBE       THE     TESTIMONY          OF    OTHERS       REGARDING

 8             OPTIONS FOR CROSSING THE COLORADO RIVER.

 9   A.        A number of witnesses, including Joshua Rhodes (Item No. 4220) and Mark Tumbough

10             (Item No. 4271) argued that the northernmost crossing of the Colorado River at Link

11             U3 would be the best option because, they argue, it is the only option that parallels

12             existing corridors.

13   Q.        DO YOU SEE ANY CONCERNS WITH THAT ARGUMENT?

14   A.        Yes. Link U3 is not the only link that crosses the Colorado River using existing

15             compatible corridors. Link J31 also crosses the Colorado River parallel to an existing

16             compatible corridor. The corridor includes five pipelines that, according to information

17             from the Texas Railroad Commission Public GIS Viewer, include three (3) pipelines

18             for crude oil, one (1) for natural/other gas, and one (1) for high volatile liquids. As

19             recently as 2017, the corridor has been disturbed, apparently to add one or more

20             pipelines.   From an environmental perspective, it is preferable to co-locate new

21             infrastructure parallel to or in close proximity to existing infrastructure corridors where

22             the land has been recently disturbed rather than locating them in previously undisturbed

23             areas. This is true even when including a safety buffer distance between the electrical

24             line and nearby pipeline.




     CROSS-REBUTTAL TESTIMONY                                                         AARON BREWER
                                                                                                      Page 5 of 14



 1           Further, in order for a route to utilize Link U3, it has to include Links G51 and Link

 2           Ul. Concerns with both of these links are addressed in my direct testimony. Also, to

 3           the extent Mr. Sansom focuses on the Colorado River impacts for his support for a Link

 4           U3 crossing, he does not address the impacts to the Lampasas River associated with

 5           any route that utilizes Link U3. Link G51 would have detrimental impacts on the

 6           Lampasas River by creating significant fragmentation of land throughout the Lampasas

 7           River watershed and would cross multiple tributaries that directly feed the Lampasas

 8           River. For example, Link G51 crosses Rocky Creek, which TPWD has designated as

 9           an ecologically significant stream segment.

10   Q.      DO YOU HAVE REBUTTAL TO OTHER EXPERT WITNESSES WHO

11           SUPPORT ROUTES INCLUDING LINKS THAT CROSS THE COLORADO

12           RIVER USING LINK J22?

13   A.      The testimony ofMr. Buntz (Item No. 4319), on behalfofa group oflandowners calling

14           themselves the Colorado River Alliance, indicates a preference for crossing the

15           Colorado River on Link J22. Mr. Buntz does not acknowledge the previous

16           infrastructure development and disturbance due to the pipelines crossing in the vicinity

17           of proposed link J31. These same two crossing areas were analyzed in a prior PUCT

18           proceeding, and the Proposal for Decision identified the crossing at C22 (the equivalent

19           of J31 in this case) was better than the crossing at C20 (the equivalent of J22 in this

20           case) because C22 (J31) crosses at an already fragmented location. 1




                Application of LCRA Transmission Services Corporation to Amend its Certificate of Convenience and
     Necessity for the Gillespie to Newton 345-kVCREZ Transmission Line in Gillespie, Llano, San Saba, Burnet, and
     Lampasas Counties , Docket No . 37448 , Proposal for Decision at 29 ( Mar . 17 , 2010)


     CROSS-REBUTTAL TESTIMONY                                                               AARON BREWER
                                                                                           Page 6 of 14


 1   III.    CROSS-REBUTTAL OF TESTIMONY REGARDING IMPACTS TO STATE
 2                                              PARKS
 3    Q.    CAN YOU DISCUSS THE IMPACT TO COLORADO BEND STATE PARK

 4          FROM THE PROPOSED LINKS?

 5   A.     Yes. Mr. Andrews testifies in support of Route 894 and discounts the impact of Route

 6          894 on state parks in vicinity to that route based on a measure of distance from the

 7          relevant state parks. However, multiple links would impact the viewshed of state parks,

 8          including links Jl 1, J27, J24, J26, and J22. Link J22 and J24 are included in Route 894.

 9          If Route 894 were approved, the transmission line would be in the foreground and

10          middleground visual zone from vantage points within the Colorado Bend State Park.

11          Research by Robert Sullivan of Argonne National Laboratory indicates that

12          transmission lines up to 500 kV in size have significant visual impacts to casual

13          observers at distances of 2.5 miles to 3 miles from vantagepoints. Further, portions of

14          Link J22 and J26 traverse steep elevations crossing hilltops in close proximity to the

15          park that will increase visibility to the park. Exhibits A and B attached to this cross-

16          rebuttal testimony depict how the proposed structures at Links J22 and J24 would be

17          visible from several locations including existing hiking trails inside Colorado Bend

18          State Park and from several locations inside the boundaries of the new Post Oak Ridge

19          State Park, as described in further detail below.

20    Q.    WHAT ABOUT POST OAK RIDGE STATE PARK?

21   A.     Post Oak Ridge is a new state park that TPWD has just started to be developed. Route

22          894 would have detrimental impacts to this park that should be avoided. Each of Links

23          Jl 1, J27, J24, J26, and J22 discussed above are within the foreground or middleground

24          visual zone of that park and in position to impact views from observation points within



      CROSS-REBUTTAL TESTIMONY                                                   AARON BREWER
                                                                                         Page 7 of 14


 1        Post Oak Ridge State Park. In fact, Links J22 and J26 are closer to Post Oak Ridge

 2        State Park than they are to Colorado Bend State Park. Each link (J22 and J26) would

 3        be prominently visible from vantage points within the park. The middleground visual

 4        zone is described by federal sources as between 0.5 mile and 3 to 5 miles from the

 5        observer. That places Link J22 either mostly or completely within the middlegroud

 6        visual zone of the Post Oak Ridge State Park where it will be noticed by observers

 7        trying to enj oy the southern views.


 8               IV.    CROSS-REBUTTAL TO WILSON MODIFICATION

 9   Q.   HAVE YOU REVIEWED THE PROPOSED MODIFICATION TO J24

10        PROPOSED BY THE WILSONS?

11   A.   Yes.

12   Q.   DO YOU HAVE ANY COMMENTS ABOUT THE MODIFICATION?

13   A.   Yes. My understanding is that this proposed modification is only in the event the final

14        order in this case selects a route that uses J24. The Wilsons still oppose Link J24 as

15        filed and still oppose it even with their proposed modification. The modification was

16        suggested as a last resort. They also oppose Link J27.

17   Q.   DOES THE MODIFICATION CHANGE YOUR ANALYSIS OF LINK J24

18        FROM THE ANALYSIS IN YOUR DIRECT TESTIMONY?

19   A.   No. Although the line would be farther from the Wilsons' house if the modification

20        were adopted, Link J24 still suffers from all the weaknesses addressed in my direct and

21        in this rebuttal testimony. And, the line would still be highly visible from the Wilsons'

22        home as they discuss in their testimonies.




     CROSS-REBUTTAL TESTIMONY                                                  AARON BREWER
                                                                                         Page 8 of 14


 1   Q.   DO YOU SEE ANY DIFFERENCE BETWEEN J24 AND J27?

 2   A.   Yes. Not only does J24 contain the Wilsons' house, the proposed right-of-way goes

 3        over an old Spanish mine where Native American remains were located.


 4   V.    CROSS-REBUTTAL OF TESTIMONY REGARDING BEST MEETS ROUTE

 5   A.   Colorado River Crossings

 6   Q.   SEVERAL EXPERT WITNESSES SUPPORT USING THE BEST MEETS

 7        ROUTE, AFTER REVIEWING THOSE OPINIONS, HAS YOUR OPINION

 8        CHANGED?
 9   A.   No. As mentioned in my testimony, and earlier in this rebuttal testimony, Links J22

10        and J26 should not be used to cross the Colorado River. The route put forth by the

11        Applicants as "best meets" (Route 894) presents significant issues that can be mitigated

12        by using instead Route 572.

13   Q.   WHAT ARE THE CONCERNS WITH CROSSING AT THOSE LOCATIONS?

14   A.   Several. These river crossings show that an angle structure would be placed close to

15        the river at both of these crossings.    Angle structures are larger, require a larger

16        foundation, and additional support. Therefore, they would cause more environmental

17        degradation than a tangent structure, such as would be placed on the crossing at J31, at

18        least on the east side of the river. As discussed above, potential crossings at Links J22

19        and J26 have been disfavored in the past and should not be used. The crossing area at

20        J31 is already disturbed, which provides an opportunity to parallel existing disturbance

21        corridors.




     CROSS-REBUTTAL TESTIMONY                                                  AARON BREWER
                                                                                             Page 9 of 14


 1   Q.   DO YOU HAVE OTHER CONCERNS WITH THE BEST MEETS ROUTE?

 2   A.   Yes. Not only is it a poor choice for the location of the river crossing, but it also utilizes

 3        Links G51 and G52, which would disrupt and fragment large swaths of land that is

 4        maintained in essentially its natural state in a manner that does not follow any

 5        infrastructure corridor or property lines. This and other reasons that Links G51 and

 6        G52 do not meet the applicable routing criteria are discussed in my direct testimony

 7        and are supported by the testimonies of the individual landowners who have also

 8        testified in this proceeding.


 9   B.   Cross-Rebuttal of Testimony Reeardine Potential Impacts on Wildlife and
10        Habitat

11   Q.   DID YOU REVIEW TESTIMONY CONCERNING POTENTIAL WILDLIFE

12        AND HABITAT IMPACTS FROM PROPOSED LINKS ON ROUTE 572?

13   A.   Yes, I did. For example, testimony of Macy Ledbetter addresses links M31, M32,

14        and M33 that are included as part of Route 572.


15   Q.   WHAT IS YOUR RESPONSE TO TESTIMONY ON THAT TOPIC?

16   A.   As noted by the Joint Applicants in the Environmental Assessment ("EA"), all

17        alternative routes would require some clearing of woody vegetation associated with

18        upland woodland and/or riparian areas. The Joint Applicants note that disturbance or

19        canopy reduction along riparian corridors in the Study Area is associated not just with

20        the San Saba River, but also the Little River, Colorado River, and South Concho River.

21                Use of Routes containing links on Route 572 can result in overall lower

22        ecological impacts for the final selected route. Some routes that cross the San Saba

23        River can mitigate the overall effects of riparian impacts, and other ecological impacts,




     CROSS-REBUTTAL TESTIMONY                                                      AARON BREWER
                                                                                       Page 10 of 14


 1        compared to other routes, including the route put forward by the Applicants as the "best

 2        meets" route.

 3               In my review of the habitats along links crossing the San Saba River, I see

 4        evidence that clearing required for construction and maintenance ofthe proposed right-

 5        of-way (ROW) will not be a dramatic change from existing conditions. There is

 6        significant disturbance from ranching activities. The native vegetation is dominated by

 7        grass and shrubs with wide spaces between trees. I measured 100 feet or more spacing

 8        commonly found between mature trees or between small groups of mature trees.

 9        Maintaining a 200-foot-wide ROW for the proposed proj ect will fit the scale of the

10        types of openings currently present in tree canopy in that area. And the ground within

11        the ROW will provide space for herbs, grasses, and low-growing fodder to support the

12        existing livestock and wildlife.


13   C.   Cross-Rebuttal of Testimony Reeardine Archeoloeical Observations

14   Q.   DID YOU REVIEW TESTIMONY REGARDING PROPOSED LINKS ON

15        ROUTE 572 AND ARCHEOLOGICAL OBSERVATIONS?

16   A.   Yes, I did. The testimony of Mark Wills addresses archeological observations on

17        Link K41, which is part of Route 572.


18   Q.   WHAT IS YOUR RESPONSE TO TESTIMONY ON THAT TOPIC?

19   A.   It is likely that unrecorded cultural sites will be identified during a future cultural

20        survey of the proposed proj ect that would follow PUCT approval of a route. The

21        Applicants explain in the EA that they intend to study the proposed proj ect area by

22        conducting a cultural resources survey and mitigate impacts to cultural resources, if

23        necessary.

     CROSS-REBUTTAL TESTIMONY                                                 AARON BREWER
                                                                                            Page ll of 14


 1                Overall, the Joint Applicants note in the EA that within the Study Area there

 2        are over 2,200 previously recorded archeological sites, with 131 of those documented

 3        as eligible for inclusion in the NHRP. The Joint Applicants also note that the overall

 4        site density and diversity indicate high archeological sensitivity in the Study Area and

 5        likelihood of encountering unrecorded cultural resources during future investigations.

 6        The Joint Applicants identify one (1) cultural site intersecting Link K41 (41SS18) that

 7        does not have an NRHP eligibility determination and two (2) cultural sites located south

 8        of the link (41 SS160 and 41SS17), one of which is determined ineligible for listing

 9        (41SS160) and the other does not have an eligibility determination. The discovery of

lo        unknown cultural resources during future survey ofthe final route is anticipated by me

11        and the Joint Applicants. It is common practice to identify and mitigate impacts to

12        cultural resources during planning and construction oftransmission lines in Texas. The

13        details provided by the witness about possible cultural sites on Link K41 does not

14        disqualify it or any associated routes from consideration.2

15                In contrast, the testimony of Ms. Kat Brown, a professor of archeology,

16        identifies numerous archeological sites on the Smith Homestead property which is

17        crossed by link G51. Ms. Brown identified numerous archeological sites on the Smith

18        Homestead property that would be impacted by the proposed project. While it is

19        commonplace for cultural sites to be identified and impacts to be mitigated during

20        construction of a line, the occurrence of several clustered sites on Link G51 can be

21        mitigated by removing Link G51 from consideration and finding alternate links or

22        using Route 572.




          2 Application at Environmental Assessment Table 7-9 of Appendix F, Table 3-13.


     CROSS-REBUTTAL TESTIMONY                                                         AARON BREWER
                                                                                            Page 12 of 14


 1        VI.        CROSS-REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF DR. MICHAEL MORRISON
 2                      REGARDING GOLDEN-CHEEKED WARBLERS

 3   Q.         DO YOU HAVE ANY CONCERNS REGARDING DR. MORRISON'S

 4              TESTIMONY REGARDING GOLDEN-CHEEKED WARBLERS?

 5              Dr. Morrison presented model data predicting the abundance of Golden-Cheeked

 6              Warblers ("GCWA") on three (3) parcels along Link J31 and conducted a survey for

 7              the birds at the same parcels. Although Dr. Morrison documents potential impacts to

 8              GCWA at Link J31, he does not document the potential impacts to GCWA from other

 9              links or routes.

lo                      Based on GCWA predicted distribution maps in his testimony, many other links

11              and routes will impact GCWA and require Endangered Species Act permits or

12              mitigation. In response to Dr. Morrison's testimony, I reviewed the predicted GCWA

13              distribution at and near Links J22, J24, G51 and G52. The Mueller Model predicts

14              GCWA concentrations near the overlook on Greenwood Creek Ranch as well as several

15              areas of predicted habitat along both Link J22, J24, G51, and G52. Removal of habitat

16              at the lookout from construction of the proj ect could sever the habitat corridor along

17              Simpson Creek linking population centers to the north and to the south. Maintaining

18              habitat integrity is one of the primary objectives of successful GCWA habitat

19              management, which is why maintaining the habitat at the Greenwood Creek Ranch

20              overlook on Link J22 is vital. Furthermore, Link G51 passes through predicted GCWA

21              habitat, with roughly 80% of the link mapped as predicted habitat, and approximately

22              5 separate clusters of higher density predicted abundance. There is a known siting on

23              link G52 and additional predicted habitat along Link G52.




     CROSS-REBUTTAL TESTIMONY                                                       AARON BREWER
                                                                                         Page 13 of 14


 1                As described in my direct testimony, the Applicant' s "best meets" route 894

 2        would impact GCWA habitat where the birds and nesting activity were recently

 3        positively identified on Link G52 and Link G51. Any of the routes including Links

 4        G51, G52, J22, or J24 are likely to impact GCWA and require an ESA permit.

 5                Without the wider evaluation of GCWA habitat, the local effects at Link J31

 6        are not put into context of the overall ecological performance ofthe final selected route.

 7        For instance, I have already pointed out in my direct and rebuttal testimony how

 8        selecting Route 572, which includes Link J31, has some ecological advantages that I

 9        will not repeat here.


10                        VII.     SUMMARY AND CONCLUSION

11   Q.   CAN YOU PROVIDE A SUMMARY OF YOUR CROSS-REBUTTAL

12        TESTIMONY?

13   A.    Yes, I can. None of the testimony I have reviewed alleviates my concerns previously

14        expressed with respect to Route 894, nor does it alter my opinion that Routes 572,295,

15        and 296 are among the routing choices that mitigate these concerns and would be

16        superior to Route 894.

17   Q.   DOES THIS CONCLUDE YOUR DIRECT TESTIMONY?

18   A.   Yes, it does.
